title: 8 Things You Shouldn’t Say to Someone With Memory Problems
author: Angela Haupt
body:
When someone develops memory problems, their loved ones often reach for the family photo album—and start quizzing them. Who’s that? Where were we? Come on, Mom, you know this one.

Dr. Carolyn Fredericks hears about this approach from people who are new to caregiving and hoping to help. They understand that staying cognitively active is important, and figure a little coaching might keep their loved one sharp. “I think this is coming from a good place,” says Fredericks, a Yale Medicine neurologist who specializes in cognitive concerns and memory disorders. “But you don’t do that by pushing on their weakness.”

Figuring out how to talk to a loved one with memory problems can take practice—and it might mean rethinking habits that once felt natural, like reminiscing about family vacations or correcting a detail they’ve gotten wrong. We asked experts which phrases to avoid, plus what to say instead to help someone feel included, respected, and at ease.

“You remember me, right?”

You might be hoping for a flash of recognition, or simply trying to offer a friendly hello. But asking someone to identify you puts them on the spot before the visit has even started, says Dr. Elizabeth Landsverk, a geriatrician and author of Living in the Moment: Overcoming Challenges and Finding Moments of Joy in Alzheimer’s Disease and Dementia.

Instead, supply the introduction yourself: “Hi, Grandma, it’s Sarah. I’m so happy to see you.” Keep it simple, rather than launching into a complicated explanation of how everyone is related. (“I’m your second cousin Susan’s granddaughter—you know, the one who moved to Arizona.”) Then give them something to talk about, like the pecan pie you brought, the flowers on the table, or the dog currently investigating your bag.

“Be in the moment,” Landsverk says. “The person can still enjoy a visit even if they don’t remember exactly who someone is.”

“I already told you that.”

You’ve answered the same question six times, you’re trying to get out the door, and your patience is wearing thin. Fredericks understands. Still, pointing out how many times you’ve supplied the information won’t necessarily help it stick.

Give them the information they need, then offer a next step you can take together. If your mom asks again what time you’re leaving for the doctor, you might say: “We’re leaving at 11. Only half an hour now—let’s get ready together.”

“Answer it as if it’s the first time you’re hearing it, even if it’s the sixth, to the extent that you possibly can,” Fredericks says.

And if you’ve already snapped? Apologize for your tone without turning the apology into another reminder of their memory problems. Fredericks suggests: “Gosh, I am so sorry. That was so rude of me. I snapped at you and I apologize, and I’ll do better next time.”

“No, that’s not what happened.”

Your dad is happily describing a beach vacation, except he’s put the wrong uncle in the rental house and moved the trip back a decade. Before jumping in, consider whether those details really need correcting.

Fredericks encourages families to focus on the feeling behind the story. You can agree that it was a wonderful trip and talk about how much fun everyone had together, without settling who slept in which bedroom. “For so many people, they might lack the details, but they keep the feeling,” she says. “And that’s what you want to connect with them on.”

How much help to offer depends on the person, Landsverk adds. Someone with early memory problems might welcome a gentle reminder that helps them finish a story. As dementia progresses, however, correcting the details can become frustrating to the person struggling. Take your cue from their response: Does the reminder help them keep going, or leave them upset?

“Don’t be silly.”

When your mom insists someone stole her purse, your instinct might be to explain why that’s impossible: You’ve been home all afternoon. Nobody came in. She probably put it somewhere.

But an explanation that seems reassuring to you can land as dismissive when someone with memory issues is frightened, Fredericks says. Start by acknowledging the distress: That sounds scary. I’ll help you look.

Recognizing the feeling doesn’t require agreeing that a theft occurred. It gives you a way to respond to what’s upsetting her without getting stuck in an argument about the evidence.

“Often they’ll kind of lose the thread of the story and just appreciate that you’re helping them calm down,” Fredericks says. “And they’ll let go of that fixation if they’re in a calmer place with you.”

“Are we ready for our bath, sweetie?”

A warm tone is welcome. Baby talk is another matter.

Kristine Williams, a professor of nursing at the University of Kansas Medical Center who studies communication with people with dementia, cautions against “elderspeak,” or language that treats an older adult like a child. That can include pet names such as “dearie,” an exaggerated, singsong voice, or substituting “we” when you mean “you.”

“‘Are we ready for our bath?’ Well, hopefully I’m not gonna be in the bath,” she says. “It kind of gives them information that they can’t act independently.”

Even affectionate language can land poorly. People using terms like “honey” and “sweetie” are often trying to show they care, Williams notes, but the words can come across as baby talk. For someone already aware of changes in their memory, being spoken to as though they’re incapable can be especially frustrating.

Context matters, of course. If you’ve called your spouse “honey” for 40 years, a diagnosis doesn’t mean you need to stop. The concern is adopting a patronizing way of speaking because someone has memory problems. “Talk to them the way you’ve always talked to them,” Williams says. “Maybe they do need you to slow down or repeat something, but that should be just based on what they need.”

“Ask her daughter. She knows.”

Your mom is sitting right next to you at Thanksgiving dinner, but your cousin turns to you to ask: Does she like the food? Would she like more potatoes? Before long, you’re having an entire conversation about her without giving her a chance to join in.

Williams encounters this dynamic in settings including doctors’ offices, where questions get directed to a companion and the person being discussed gets left out. Even when someone needs help supplying details, keep addressing them and inviting their input. “You may not ask them 20 questions,” she says, but it’s “really important to keep them involved and not left out of the conversation.”

Fredericks suggests bringing another person into the conversation naturally. If your mom is struggling to recall a trip you took together, for example, you could turn to your sister and say: Tanya, you were on that trip too. What was your favorite part? That lets someone else contribute without drawing attention to what your mom can’t recall.

People can still recognize when they’re being brushed aside. “Just as anyone else would be,” Fredericks says, “you would feel ashamed or slighted or hurt by that kind of talk.”

“What do you want to do today?”

You want your loved one to have a say in how they spend their day. But for a person with more advanced cognitive difficulties, a question as broad as “What do you want to do today?” can be overwhelming, Landsverk says.

Offer a couple of concrete possibilities instead: Would you like to take a walk or listen to some music? Getting dressed can work the same way. Hold up two shirts and ask which they’d prefer. “You definitely want to give them choices,” Landsverk says. “But make it simple.”

And let their tastes surprise you. Maybe your mom always dressed to the nines, but now she’s drawn to anything pink and sparkly. You don’t need to steer her toward the understated blouse she would have chosen 10 years ago. “Things change,” Landsverk says. “You have to figure out—it’s not what you think Mom should have. It’s like, what does Mom like to do now?”

“Come on, everyone wants to see you!”

The whole family has gathered for the holidays, and your loved one wants to retreat to another room. You might be tempted to coax them back: Everyone came all this way. Surely they can stay a little longer.

“I love having 12, 20 people around, but that might be too much for Mom now,” Landsverk says. Instead of insisting they rejoin the crowd, ask: Would you like to go somewhere quieter?

Set aside a room where relatives can stop in for short visits, one or two at a time. Your loved one might enjoy catching up with a grandchild, come out for pie, and then be ready to call it a day. “After a couple hours, if she’s seeming tired, let her go rest,” Landsverk says.

That same flexibility helps beyond the holidays. If a favorite restaurant has become too noisy, try takeout at home or a picnic in the park. “You can go do something special, but you cut down the noise,” she says. “You cut down the amount of people and the pressure.”

Sometimes, slowing down makes the visit better for everyone. While visiting patients in their homes, Landsverk usually had another appointment to get to. But one warm fall afternoon, a delay in her schedule left her with extra time to chat with a small group of people with dementia. She still remembers the sunlight bursting through the leaves. “We had a very pleasant conversation back and forth,” she says. “Not all of it made sense, but the experience was nice for all of us.”
